catalog_quote: [p. 58, 5.4.1 General features] The tone system is essentially a two tone system with downstep and upstep. It could be called a "see-saw system" more appropriately than a downstep system. Thus the downstepping influence which characterises other Kwa languages and especially Igbo, is counteracted by widely distributed raising influences. The tone system comprises: Two basic tones: High (H or ´), Low (L or) Three features: Downstep (!) Upstep (^) Latent Low ( before the word) ... new_statements.quote: [p. 58, §5.4.1] The tone system is essentially a two tone system with downstep and upstep. It could be called a "see-saw system" more appropriately than a downstep system. [...] Many minimal tone pairs and triplets are found, and some quadruplets [...] [p. 34, §3.3.3] This reduction in the glides leads to the development of a certain type of rhythm. This occurs in sequences involving glides which are then reduced to a succession of raised highs and highs with a compensatory stress accompanying the raised high tone or the high tone. The faster the speed of the spans, the more this rhythm develops. [p. 46, §4.3, phonological word] There are two demarcative features, vowel elision and the loss of syllabicity of the nasal with nasalisation, and one non-demarcative feature, vowel harmony.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Izi is described as a tone language (H vs L, with downstep, upstep and a latent low; lexical minimal tone pairs/quadruplets). No word stress or word accent is posited: the phonological word is defined by syllable-structure templates, vowel elision at word borders, nasal (de)syllabicity and vowel harmony only. The sole mention of 'stress' is a phrase-level (tone-span) rhythmic effect in fast conversational register, where reduced tone glides leave a compensatory stress on (raised) high-toned syllables; i.e. stress is treated as a by-product of tone realisation, not as a lexical or positionally fixed word property.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The rhythmic compensatory stress is said to increase with speech tempo and to be a Register-1 (conversational) phenomenon absent from the Deliberate register (p. 36).
new_statements.domain_note: The stress remark concerns the tone span (a phrase-level unit above the phonological word) in connected fast speech, documented with instrumental pitch tracings (pp. 36-40); no statement locates stress within the word or in citation forms. Hierarchy used: utterance > pause group > tone span > phonological word > syllable.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Meier, Meier & Bendor-Samuel 1975 describe Izi proper (Glottolog dialect izii1239, ISO izz), based on fieldwork 1964-1971 at Abia Unufu (ebya unuphu) c. 10 miles south of Abakaliki; the authors state Izi has no internal dialects and forms a 'North-eastern Igbo' cluster with Ezaa (ezaa1238), Ikwo (ikwo1238) and probably Mgbo (mgbo1238) and Ishielu (c. 95% lexicostatistic similarity among Izi/Ezaa/Ikwo). The catalog key izie1238 is the cluster-level language; the statement strictly covers the Izi member.

sources.note: Part I Phonology (chs. 2-6, pp. 29-84) read: Izi is a two-tone (H, L) system with downstep, upstep and latent low (5.4.1 p. 58), many tonal minimal pairs. The phonological-word chapter (ch. 4, pp. 41-54) gives word structure and lists only vowel elision, loss of nasal syllabicity and vowel harmony as word-level features; no word stress or accent is posited anywhere.
